speaker: Lisa Blatt
title: Arguing In Front of SCOTUS | Interview: Lisa Blatt
question: At the U.S. Supreme Court, why does heavy emergency-docket intervention persist despite straining the justices?
guest: Just more broadly on the interim docket, I do think it's not great for the court. It's changing the vibe. It changes the schedules. It changes their mood. It changes the types of cases they take. It's bad. I wish they had less of it, and I think the court is finally getting a little exhausted. It doesn't mean that they won't keep taking cases because—sorry, court, but you're very into your power, so there's no way they will ever resist taking a case if it's important enough. They're just not willing to sit on the sidelines, and the leaks on the West Virginia case kind of confirm all that. So a little bit they don't have much of a choice, but I think they would be very happy if it decreased a little bit so they could go on some summer vacations, relax a little bit, and take the temperature down. My guess is they're a little exhausted from the emergency interim docket.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Heavy emergency-docket intervention persists because the forces driving it are structural, and the justices themselves have chosen to keep responding to them.

On the demand side, presidents increasingly govern through executive action rather than legislation, and challengers respond by seeking sweeping injunctions from favorable district courts. When a lower court blocks a major policy nationwide, the government, of whichever party, asks the Supreme Court for immediate relief, and the solicitor general now files such applications far more often than in past decades. Capital cases and election disputes add time-sensitive filings.

On the supply side, a majority of the Court has shown it is willing to grant relief. It treats a blocked government policy as a form of irreparable harm and views declining to act as itself a consequential decision, since whichever side loses at the interim stage may live with that outcome for years while litigation proceeds. Each grant signals to litigants that asking is worthwhile, inviting more applications.

No external check interrupts this cycle: the Court controls its own docket, Congress has not restricted interim relief, and the majority regards intervention as necessary rather than optional, despite complaints about thin briefing and rushed, sparsely explained rulings.

points.why: The response explains why emergency filings increase but never connects that workload to changes in the Court’s merits case selection.
The response mentions rushed rulings and thin briefing but does not connect the emergency workload to exhaustion among the justices.
The response portrays the majority as unwilling to leave high-stakes interim outcomes in place because those outcomes can determine which policy governs for years.

views declining to act as itself a consequential decision
the majority regards intervention as necessary rather than optional

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Heavy emergency-docket intervention persists because structural timing pressures, litigation tactics, and the Supreme Court’s own doctrine lock the justices and litigants into a self-reinforcing cycle. Modern presidents govern aggressively through executive action, which challengers quickly halt in favorable district courts. Even after *Trump v. CASA* (2025) curbed universal injunctions, plaintiffs pivoted to class actions and Administrative Procedure Act stays to secure sweeping blocks. Because ordinary merits litigation takes years, preliminary orders can outlast much of a presidential term, turning interim rulings into de facto final outcomes. Confronted with that reality, the Court’s majority treats halting a sovereign law or federal policy as nearly automatic irreparable harm, making emergency stays turn largely on early merits predictions rather than traditional procedural restraint. Each grant then fuels demand: once the Solicitor General and state officials see the Court repeatedly rescue blocked policies, seeking immediate intervention becomes routine strategy, leaving neither government litigants nor a majority wary of lower-court overreach willing to step back.

The response describes routine emergency filings without connecting the workload to exhaustion, morale, or reduced recovery time for the justices.
The response attributes continued intervention to a majority unwilling to leave consequential interim decisions in the hands of lower courts.

noweb.answer:
Heavy emergency-docket intervention persists because structural incentives in modern litigation make restraint costly for a majority of the justices. As presidents govern aggressively through unilateral executive action, challengers routinely turn to sympathetic forums to obtain rapid preliminary relief—through sweeping injunctions, class actions, or Administrative Procedure Act vacaturs—that halts major federal policies immediately. Because ordinary merits appeals take years, refusing to step in can let a single district judge or circuit panel freeze national policy or trigger irreversible real-world effects for much of an administration's term.

Doctrinal and institutional dynamics reinforce that pressure. By centering stay decisions on likely merits success and treating blocks on government policies as inherent sovereign harm, the Court has turned emergency applications into early merits tests and a mechanism for policing lower-court compliance. That approach rewards the Solicitor General and other litigants for seeking immediate relief whenever lower courts diverge from the majority's jurisprudence, locking even overburdened justices into a self-reinforcing cycle they are unwilling to unilaterally abandon.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Heavy emergency-docket intervention persists mainly because the incentives keep producing it, even though the justices find it draining.

**Demand keeps rising.** Since 2025 the Trump administration has filed emergency applications at an unusual pace. Its aggressive executive actions draw quick injunctions from district courts, and the Solicitor General often asks the Court to step in before the courts of appeals rule.

**Wins invite more filings.** The conservative majority has usually granted the government stays, so it keeps applying. Challengers, for their part, now rely on class actions and challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) after *Trump v. CASA* (2025) limited universal injunctions. That keeps the flow coming from both sides.

**The majority thinks intervening is its duty.** Justices like Kavanaugh argue that someone must decide which side bears the harm while a case is pending, because full merits review takes months or years. They have also told lower courts to follow these "interim" orders as precedent, which makes the docket more consequential and gives litigants more reason to use it.

The cost is real. Justices describe exhaustion and rushed decisions with little explanation, and Kagan, Sotomayor and Jackson have dissented sharply. But no rule forces the Court to cut back, and the majority prefers controlling outcomes now to waiting.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Heavy emergency-docket intervention persists because structural pressures in American governance and the justices’ own incentives lock the Court into a feedback loop. Amid congressional gridlock, presidents rely heavily on sweeping executive actions, while states enact fast-moving, contentious policies. Challengers routinely seek rapid preliminary injunctions in sympathetic trial courts, halting major programs before full litigation unfolds. Because the Court’s ordinary merits process takes months or years—often outlasting a policy, program, or election cycle—deciding who prevails in the interim frequently settles the real-world stakes.

Meanwhile, a majority of justices is unwilling to leave lower-court orders it views as legally erroneous in effect while appeals slowly proceed. By treating likely merits outcomes as decisive and granting interim relief more readily, the Court lowers the threshold for intervention. That receptiveness, paired with brief orders giving lower judges limited guidance, encourages the Solicitor General, states, and private litigants to seek emergency relief whenever they lose below—sustaining the workload despite the strain it imposes.

The response mentions workload strain in general terms without linking recurring off-cycle petitions to exhaustion, lower morale, or reduced recovery time.
The response portrays a majority as unwilling to let lower-court rulings it considers erroneous control the outcome while consequential disputes remain on appeal.

Heavy emergency-docket intervention persists because waiting for a full appeal can effectively decide who wins. When a lower court blocks a federal policy, months of delay can consume much of the time an administration has to carry it out. When a policy remains in force, people challenging it may suffer harms that a later ruling can’t undo. Both sides therefore have strong incentives to seek immediate relief, especially when a single injunction has nationwide effects.

The justices face the same timing problem. Denying a stay leaves the lower court’s ruling in force, while granting one can let a policy operate for months before the Court reaches the merits. Either choice can have lasting consequences. The strain falls on the Court, but the stakes in each case keep litigants asking and give the justices reasons to intervene.

A lower-court injunction can halt a federal policy nationwide, and allowing a challenged policy to take effect can cause harms that a later ruling cannot undo. The workload falls on the Court, but each application arrives as a separate, time-sensitive decision. That makes it easier for the justices to keep intervening case by case than to agree on a general rule for intervening less.

Heavy emergency-docket intervention persists because waiting for a final ruling can effectively decide what happens on the ground. A policy can be blocked for years while appeals proceed, or it can take effect and cause harm that a later ruling cannot undo. Some justices, including Brett Kavanaugh, see emergency orders as a way to prevent those harms and give the country a uniform answer about which rules apply while litigation continues. The Trump administration has repeatedly sought emergency relief when lower courts block its policies, and the Supreme Court’s conservative majority has often granted it. Those wins give the administration and other litigants reason to keep asking. The result is a cycle in which the practical stakes of waiting and the demonstrated payoff of filing keep cases coming, even as tight deadlines crowd out the justices’ regular work.
